source.title: Rethinking Benign Relearning: Syntax as the Hidden Driver of Unlearning Failures
source.authors: Sangyeon Yoon; Hyesoo Hong; Wonje Jeung; Albert No

record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests benign relearning after unlearning and argues that recovery depends more consistently on syntactic similarity than topical relevance; it also tests syntactic diversification as a counter-method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports many additional curves and appendix analyses. Rows below retain the explicit findings and tabulated results most directly bearing on recovery, template injection, and diversification. Cited findings from prior work are not recorded as rows. Figure-only evidence is identified as such.
record.test_reason: The study runs benign-relearning attacks on GA, NPO and SCRUB unlearned models (TOFU, WHP, WMDP). It argues the topical-relevance account of recovery is insufficient and that syntactic similarity drives it. It also runs a template-prefill prompt attack and tests a counter-method, syntactic diversification.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that syntactic similarity, not topical relevance, is the main driver of benign relearning: standard unlearning suppresses answer templates more than keywords, and shared syntax restores them. They also show that syntactic diversification of the forget set suppresses relearning, speeds forgetting and improves utility. They add that refusal-style safety training is even more vulnerable and that LoRA relearning amplifies recovery.
record.recipe_differences: Uses established GA, NPO, and SCRUB unlearning approaches, but tests a different mechanism of benign relearning centered on syntax and introduces syntactic diversification; it does not reproduce the original studies' full attack recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery varies with relearn-set syntax, unlearning method, unlearning step/checkpoint, and in the WHP/WMDP analyses whether syntax matches the target data or evaluation queries. The paper also reports stronger recovery with LoRA-based than full-parameter relearning.

fits_no_version.finding: Safety-training methods (IDK, DPO) are far more vulnerable to syntactic relearning than GA/NPO, nearly fully recovering within a few steps (Section E, Fig 16).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-based safety training used as unlearning only masks knowledge and is more vulnerable to benign relearning than gradient-based unlearning.

record.problems: Many core results are presented as figures without numerical values in the text. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates. The WHP topical relearn set contains direct or partial target answers, so it is not a clean benign-relearning comparison. Some reported comparisons use synthetic TOFU facts and generated relearn data.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted separate curve values from Figures 2-4, 8, 10-14, and 16 where values are not stated numerically in the text; omitted additional metric-specific rows from Appendix H beyond the keyword results in Table 7, although the paper says the metrics agree. Appendix B.3.1 also reports full-parameter and LoRA relearning comparisons, and Appendix G.4 compares diversification generators; not extracted as separate rows.

untested.parts: Near-chance accuracy and preserved general ability are not reported for the attacked standard-unlearning checkpoints.
No activation-direction ablation. Only template-injection and loss-ratio analyses.
Rephrasing, jailbreaks, translation and in-context facts not tested. Only the answer-prefix template injection is tested.

Diversification tested only on TOFU with GA, against syntactic relearning and template injection. Not tested against other relearn sets, ablation, quantization or other prompt attacks, nor on WHP or WMDP.

missing.what: BLUR re-analysis: Dmid and Dlow (Lorem Ipsum) relearn sets recover nearly as much as Dhi under best-step evaluation. ROUGE-L is roughly 0.16–0.32 against an unlearned 0.00 on WMDP and WHP, and about 0.12–0.43 against 0.02–0.04 on RWKU. This bears on B (unrelated data).
Phi-1.5B TOFU model: syntactic relearning restores forgotten names under GA, NPO and SCRUB.
Full-parameter unlearning followed by full or LoRA relearning: syntactic sets still recover more than topical ones, and LoRA relearning recovers faster.
Metric-specific Top-190 syntactic relearn sets give RSR 0.6–0.8 across unlearning steps 31–50.
Per-method relearn success on the target, topical and syntactic sets (e.g., GA: syntactic 1.00 vs topical 0.00).
IDK and DPO safety-training models nearly fully recover under syntactic relearning.
Diversification done with Llama-3-8B gives nearly the same relearning resistance as GPT-4o.

record.verdict_notes: The reader used V1–V6, which map to versions A–F. Table 7 does not name the unlearning method; it is likely GA. The template injection (R18) is an answer-prefill prompt, so it is linked to E as well as C. For the counter-method rows, states are given relative to F (observed = resistance holds), not relative to recovery. No uncertainty estimates are reported, and many results are figure-only. The study is not one of the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports suppression and subsequent recovery, but does not establish that the original unlearning methods reach near chance while preserving general ability in the same attack comparison.
The reported recovery uses benign relearning sets with syntactic overlap; this does not test recovery from a few unrelated examples generally, or relearning directly on subsets of forgotten facts.
No activation-direction ablation is tested. The internal-mechanism evidence is about template suppression and keyword leakage, including a template-injection test.
Prompt rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, and in-context information as recovery attacks are not tested.
Syntactic diversification is tested against syntactic relearning, not against activation ablation, quantization, or prompting-only attacks.

relation.reason: It runs its own relearning and prefill attacks and reports recovery results on versions A, B, C, E and F.

tranche.reason: The study argues the topical-relevance account of benign relearning is incomplete and restates it as syntactic similarity.

source_check.notes: Table 7 (R5-R12) is at 50 unlearning steps with LoRA unlearning by default (B.1) and names no unlearning method. Figures 4, 8, 14 and 17 are figure-only; Figure 15 WMDP values are plot labels scored by a GPT-4o judge. Diversification is the authors' own method, tested with GA on TOFU Llama-2-7b-chat; no code, no uncertainty.

statements.correction: Table 7 (50 unlearning steps, method not named): the syntactic set gives keyword RSR 0.8 at relearning step 23. Retrained-model control is 0% at every step for both sets (Table 5). WMDP (Zephyr-7b-beta, GA) relearn sets contain no direct eval answers. No code, no uncertainty.

Topical TOFU set keyword RSR 0.0 at relearning steps 11-47, at 50 unlearning steps (Table 7). The WHP topical set (BLUR Dhi) holds direct or partial answers to 5 of 10 target questions and shows little relearning effect (Appendix C).
Table 7: topical set RSR 0.0 vs syntactic set 0.8 at relearning step 23. The syntactic set has no target answers (retrained-model control 0%).

Appendix H: keyword, cosine-similarity and LLM-judge metrics have Pearson correlations of 0.992-0.997 (Table 6). At step 11: keyword 0.2, cosine 0.2488, judge 0.3 (Table 7). The authors call their conclusions stable across metrics.
statements.problem: The prose says nothing about this study, but it cites R9 as evidence that the measure changes whether recovery shows. The study reports the opposite: its three leakage metrics agree.

statements.correction: Table 7: syntactic set keyword RSR 0.8 at relearning step 23 vs topical set 0.0 (50 unlearning steps).
